How long is the object? Give your answer in cm.

A rectangle has sides 9 cm and 9 cm. What is its perimeter?

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The perimeter items that exist are sound and correctly keyed: seed 42, 'A triangle has sides 2 cm, 1 cm, and 2 cm. What is its perimeter?', keys '5'; seed 603, 'A square has a side of 3 cm. What is its perimeter?', keys '12'; and seed 601, 'How much fencing is needed to go all the way around it?', keys '42' for the garden it describes. But only seven of the fifteen samples involve a perimeter at all, and the tools clause is never met on a figure, because no sample asks a student to measure the sides of a figure with a ruler and then total them.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: The sentence names identifying, measuring, and appropriate tools, and only the computing of a perimeter is really covered. Identifying is absent: nothing asks which measurement is the perimeter or asks a student to trace the boundary of a figure, and the nearest thing is the wording at seed 601, 'How much fencing is needed to go all the way around it?'. Measuring with an appropriate tool is present only in the wrong place: seeds 44, 45, 500, 501 and 502 all read 'How long is the object? Give your answer in cm.', which is a ruler read of the length of one object, never the perimeter of a plane figure. Two of the three named sub-cases are therefore not covered.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: The structure suits Grade 2 Quarter 4. Seed 604, 'A triangle has sides 2 cm, 4 cm, and 4 cm.', is a three-addend sum; seed 43, 'A rectangle has sides 5 cm and 12 cm.', needs each side counted twice; and the largest total in the packet, at seed 601, is '42'. No formula notation appears, no multiplication shortcut is required, and there are no decimals or fractions anywhere in the packet.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Figure variety is reasonable, with a triangle at seed 42 and seed 604, a rectangle at seed 43 and seed 46, a square at seed 603, and a real-world item at seed 601. Both triangles can exist: at seed 42, 'A triangle has sides 2 cm, 1 cm, and 2 cm.', the two shorter sides sum to more than the longest, and at seed 604, 'A triangle has sides 2 cm, 4 cm, and 4 cm.', likewise. Two things weaken it. Five samples repeat one identical stem, 'How long is the object? Give your answer in cm.', and seed 51, 'A rectangle has sides 9 cm and 9 cm. What is its perimeter?', presents a square under the name rectangle while seed 603 names a square outright, which reads as inconsistent at this grade.

competency_alignment.rationale: Eight of the fifteen samples address a different competency entirely, with no plane figure and no boundary in sight. Seed 605 asks 'Which unit would you use to measure the distance between the barangay hall and the plaza: centimeters or meters?' and keys 'm'; seed 606 asks 'Which is longer: 1 cm or 6 cm?' and keys '6'; seed 607 asks 'The distance from the bench to the tree is 2 m. The distance from the gate to the tree is 3 m. Which distance is longer?' and keys '3'. Add the five ruler reads of 'How long is the object? Give your answer in cm.' and the majority of this node is Quarter 2 length-and-distance content standing on a node whose sentence is about the perimeter of a plane figure.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Where a thing is named the unit fits it well: seed 601, 'A rectangular garden is 11 m long and 10 m wide.', uses meters for a garden, and the figure sides stay in centimeters throughout. The ruler items are where it breaks. Seeds 500, 501 and 502 all ask 'How long is the object? Give your answer in cm.' with keys in the sixties and eighties of centimeters, longer than the classroom ruler such an item implies, and because the stem names nothing beyond 'the object' neither the choice of tool nor the fit of unit to thing can be checked. Seed 46, 'A rectangle has sides 7 cm and 1 cm.', is a sliver a Grade 2 child would struggle to measure.
